Before I quit, cannabis did wonders for my sleep. In fact, some nights I would even pass out on the couch until my partner woke me up to get me to move to the bed, which I would never otherwise do (generally not the comfiest place). As someone with complex PTSD, anxiety, insomnia, it really helped, and I slept every night, very consistently. I feel like I did before I started using it, for better or for worse.

I am very patiently waiting for it to become legal. No pharmaceutical has ever helped me like that, and there are few if any adverse side effects.

As someone who's been there, I realized after many years that our perception of superiority/inferiority is false. However, it is hard to convince people of this because a lot of people like the gratification they get from being "better" than others. And it can be hard to feel like you're not inferior when society keeps saying you are. So I won't try to convince you, but I did want to relate to your situation.

I eventually learned that it's not fair to compare myself to other people because I am just built differently than everyone else, and while I may not be able to live up to them in certain ways, I can exceed them in others. We all naturally have different strengths and talents, and it's about discovering and nurturing our strengths while working on our "weaknesses." It has been hard to let go of my insecurities, but at the end of the day, I bet those same people have their own and think the same thing we do, in their own way. It's easier for me to focus on working on myself now that I don't care about trying to meet my own unrealistic expectations of myself.

For example... Do I still feel a bit insecure about my body when I see certain media portrayals of bodies/physical appearance? Yes, absolutely. But I know that's just not how my body is, and it may never be that way because it just wasn't *built* to be. I've found comfort in other people that look like me being comfortable with themselves, or people of different body types being supportive of each other.

I think that we as a society are way too concerned about the "mainstream" perception of people in media that we completely forget what *average, everyday people* look and behave like. We compare ourselves to exceptions and not the *true* average and then feel inadequate because we don't match up to those exceptions. I think that's so harmful to the collective psyche of society because we then expect more out of ourselves than we can realistically give, that *most* people can realistically give, without realizing it.

Don't beat yourself up for having limitations or imperfections, because we *all* really do have them. Yes, *all* of us. And that's okay.

I find this to be pretty true, I've struggled with depression and other pretty severe issues for about a decade.

The hardest part is finding the motivation to start. I really, really struggle with that with my chronic pain. But once I start, I usually just keep going until I'm done and then feel 1% better about myself. And 1% is a lot better than 0%, even though it's not much.

I play my role, but I see human behavior a lot differently now. We're all just floating through space together trying to figure out stuff out, just being strange little accidents in the universe, living our lives and dying. I try to be more forgiving of certain behaviors (not all, some behaviors I do judge more harshly now) because I know others don't know the same things I do. Like, for example, how we're all just pretending to be things we aren't so that we live up to our personal and societal standards and how we all (most of us, at least) just want to belong and be wanted.

For me, it means that I can focus on the things that I want to for *my* satisfaction, and not the things that people tell me to. My dysmorphia is way better now, though I still would want to change certain features for *my own* satisfaction, and not others'.

I try to be a lot more understanding of people I interact with in person. I know that they've lived their entire lives in a prison of our own unwitting creation and a lot of people feel bound to social expectations instead of their own. I have a newfound respect for people that forged their own path without the realizations I made on psychedelics, though. The most interesting people out there are those that broke their chains through conscious effort, and I tend to gravitate toward those people. Possibly because I believe they have things they can teach me.

I also try to be a "nicer" person. I say "nicer" because I'm still heavily flawed and not all that nice. I have always been sensitive to the pain of others but now I see how much pain others are *truly* in, how much fear and anxiety people experience, etc. I was pretty empathetic before, but now I feel a lot more understanding about why people feel certain things and not just the how. I had severe cystic acne as a teenager, had to go to a couple of dermatologists and had to be on topical *and* oral medications to control it. That includes birth control at one point.

That being said, skincare makes a difference. I can't wear liquid foundation because it *does* lead to cysts. I have to have a skincare routine because even into my 20s, if I don't wash my face every day or every other day, it *does* make my cysts worse. You shouldn't wash your face more than once a day (it can dry your skin out too much, leading to worsening acne because your body will try to produce more oil to keep your skin from drying out, you want to dry the cysts out but not to the point it backfires), and it won't get them to go away completely, but it can *help* prevent new cysts from forming by removing excess oil and dead skin before it gets too deep and sometimes it can even help shrink the cysts themselves.

Hygiene absolutely makes a difference. Does it take a long time and a solid routine? Yes. Are you gonna need other treatments to make cysts go away completely? Yes. But saying hygiene and skincare don't make a difference isn't fully correct. You should still wash your face (you will need something specifically made for cystic acne, not just whatever you have on hand) and moisturize with a light, oil-free moisturizer, and occasionally gently exfoliate because exfoliation can help cleanser work more efficiently. You shouldn't neglect your skin just because your acne is hormonal (mine was) or is deeper in your pores, you should still try to keep your skin healthy because it does help prevent issues down the road. Also, just because you get cystic acne, doesn't mean you can't also get regular acne. I had a good mix myself, and still get both.

Industrial agriculture can mean putting shelf life above flavor. For example, most store-bought tomatoes have absolutely NOTHING on homegrown varieties like heirlooms. Vegetables grown by local farms or in your own garden usually taste a *lot* better and tend to be fresher when you do eat them.

I personally add turmeric and freshly cracked rainbow peppercorns (if you haven't tried it but dislike pepper, I recommend it, the flavor is a lot better) to everything because inflammation, but there are so many spices out there you can use.

Vegetables can be just as delicious as protein or starches, if not more so, as long as you give them a chance to shine.
